passage: Last year I nearly missed the Class 10 trip to the hill fort. I'm Reena, I use a wheelchair, and my father, Manoj, had already told the class teacher I wouldn't go, before asking me. He had also decided I'd take commerce instead of science because the labs are upstairs, and he checked my phone location twice a day. I knew it was love, and fear of me getting hurt. But I felt like a parcel being posted around. One night I finally said, "Papa, you keep deciding my life in the kitchen without me." He went quiet for a long time. The next day we called the school together. The teacher found a ramped route to the fort's lower gate, and Papa agreed I'd go with a friend and a charged phone. I went. I got sunburnt and took my best photo ever. We've started talking about science too.

qa.q: What did Manoj tell the class teacher before asking Reena?
qa.a: He told the teacher that Reena wouldn't go on the trip.

qa.q: How did Reena feel about decisions being made without asking, and what words show it?
qa.a: Reena felt smothered and frustrated, like a parcel being posted around, while still knowing it came from love.

qa.q: What turning point helped the family respect Reena's growing independence?
qa.a: Speaking up to Papa, then calling the school together so a ramped route and a safe plan with a friend could be made.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt hearing that he kept deciding Reena's life without asking?
qa.a: Manoj was probably hurt and shaken, then thoughtful, since he had acted out of love and fear.

grounding: Shows a disabled teenager feeling smothered when a loving, fearful parent decides everything, and involvement in decisions with a safe risk respecting her autonomy.

passage:
Friday, 9 p.m.
Went to the passport office with Rajni today. Three things.
One: the counter is on the first floor. No lift, no ramp. A guard said, "Madam can wait here, your friend can go up." Madam cannot, because it's my passport.
Two: when they finally sent an officer down, he looked at Rajni the whole time. "What is her date of birth?" Rajni kept pointing at me until he got it.
Three: an aunty in the queue patted my head and said, "So brave, beta." I was renewing a passport, not climbing a mountain.
I cried in the auto. Then Rajni said, "None of that was about you. It's their stairs." That helped. Tomorrow I'm writing to the office asking for a ground-floor counter.
Gopika

qa.q: Where was the passport counter?
qa.a: On the first floor, with no lift and no ramp.

qa.q: Why did Gopika cry in the auto?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and worn out after being blocked, talked over and pitied all day.

qa.q: What fair action does Gopika plan, and why does it fit?
qa.a: Writing to the office to ask for a ground-floor counter, because the stairs are a barrier in the building, not a failing in her.

qa.q: How does Rajni see what happened that day?
qa.a: Rajni sees the problems as the office's barriers, not Gopika's fault, and keeps redirecting the officer to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult with a disability meeting stairs, being talked past and pitied, and recognising these as barriers in the world that call for fair action.

passage: Uday, you asked how I stay so calm about my hospital mornings. I'm Alka, and I wasn't calm at twenty-five. That was the year my kidneys gave up and dialysis took three mornings of every week. I had a ticket for a trek in Ladakh that I never used. Some days I sat in the car park and cried for that trip. Some days I wanted to throw the machine out of the window because I was too tired to finish one report. And some days, sometimes the very same day, I felt proud that I'd learned the whole routine myself and still handed in my work. My mother kept telling me to "stay positive". It made me feel I was failing at feelings too. Then a nurse told me all three were allowed. That helped more than anything anyone said.

qa.q: What trip did Alka never take?
qa.a: A trek in Ladakh.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Alka have that year, and what shows each?
qa.a: Grief, crying in the car park over the trip; frustration, wanting to throw out the machine; and pride in learning the routine and still handing in work.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped Alka most, and why?
qa.a: The nurse saying all three feelings were allowed, because it stopped Alka feeling like a failure at feelings too.

qa.q: How might Alka's mother have meant "stay positive"?
qa.a: Alka's mother probably meant it lovingly, hoping to protect Alka, without seeing that it made Alka feel judged for the grief.

grounding: Illustrates a person living with long-term illness feeling grief, frustration and pride on the same day, with all of them treated as valid.

subtype: Partner, friend or employer supporting well [Response]
passage:
Monday: Kavitha told Anirban, her team lead, that her illness had flared and mornings were hard. He didn't sigh or call her brave. He asked, "What would actually help? You tell me." She asked for an eleven o'clock start for two weeks.
Thursday: The client call had been moved to noon without anyone mentioning why. When a colleague joked, "Must be nice to come in late," Anirban said evenly, "It's agreed. Let's get to the slides."
Two weeks later: Kavitha said she felt ready for ten o'clock again. Anirban nodded, put it in the calendar, and asked if the Thursday noon slot still suited her. It did. She finished the quarterly report a day early, and nobody made a speech about it.

qa.q: What start time did Kavitha ask for?
qa.a: An eleven o'clock start, for two weeks.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt when Anirban asked what would help?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and respected, since he let her decide instead of pitying her or treating her as a burden.

qa.q: Which of Anirban's actions show good support?
qa.a: Asking what help she wanted, quietly moving the call, calmly shutting down the joke, and checking in again without fuss.

qa.q: What would change for Kavitha if Anirban had praised her as "so brave" in front of everyone?
qa.a: She might feel singled out and uneasy, turned into an inspiration story instead of treated as a normal colleague.

grounding: Shows an employer asking what help is wanted, adapting plans without fuss and treating an ill colleague neither as an inspiration nor as a burden.

passage:
"The plaster stays on till after the race?" Damini stared at her arm. "The inter-school race is so soon!"
"I know," said Papa Lokesh, sitting on the edge of her bed. "It's rotten luck."
"It's not luck, it's that stupid swing. I hate it." Her lip shook. "Will my arm be bent forever?"
"The doctor showed us the X-ray, remember? The bone is in a straight line. It will knit back."
"But I'll be slow when I come back. Everyone will beat me."
"Maybe at first. So let's make small goals. This week, you learn to write your name with your left hand."
"That's silly."
"Is it? Bet you can't do it."
Damini narrowed her eyes, grabbed a pencil and started. "Watch me."

qa.q: What small goal does Papa suggest for this week?
qa.a: Learning to write her name with her left hand.

qa.q: What was Damini worried about, apart from missing the race?
qa.a: She was scared her arm would stay bent and worried that everyone would beat her when she came back.

qa.q: Which parts of Papa's response help Damini's mind heal too?
qa.a: He agrees it's rotten luck, gives honest information from the X-ray, and turns her energy to a small goal she can achieve.

qa.q: How might Papa Lokesh feel seeing Damini's lip shake?
qa.a: He probably feels sad for her and protective, which is why he stays calm and turns it into a playful challenge.

grounding: Shows a child with a broken arm feeling angry, scared and worried about the future, and comfort, honest information and a small goal helping her mind heal.

passage:
Week one: Gargi watched the district hockey trials from the stands with her knee in a brace. When the coach put Aditi in her position, Gargi went home and didn't touch her phone all evening. "Who am I if I'm not playing?" she wrote in her notebook.
Week three: Aditi texted, "We need someone to track the other team's corners. Coach asked for you." Gargi went, clipboard in hand, and found she liked spotting patterns. She also did every exercise the doctor had set, even the boring ones.
Week seven: Back on the field for light drills, Gargi saw Aditi still in her spot. It stung. But at the break Aditi said, "Your corner notes won us the semi." Gargi grinned.

qa.q: What job did the coach ask Gargi to do in week three?
qa.a: Tracking the other team's corners.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling in week one, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt lost, low and afraid of being replaced; she ignored her phone and wrote, "Who am I if I'm not playing?"

qa.q: What helped Gargi through the injury?
qa.a: Staying part of the team through the corner notes, finding a new interest in spotting patterns, and doing every exercise the doctor set.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel about taking Gargi's position?
qa.a: Aditi may feel a little awkward about it, which could be why she keeps including Gargi and praises her notes.

grounding: Shows a teenage athlete sidelined by injury feeling lost and afraid of being replaced, and staying part of the team, a new interest and medical advice protecting her.

passage: Irfan, sit down, you're limping and don't tell me you're not. Let your old uncle Joseph tell you about the summer I was sixteen. I sprained my ankle two weeks before the district football final. The coach said rest. But I could smell that trophy. So I wrapped it tight, told everyone it was fine, and ran on it every evening behind the church. On the day of the final I lasted twenty minutes. Then something went snap, and I spent that match, and the whole next season, on the bench. The worst part? When I finally told the coach, he just said, "Why didn't you tell me? I'd have planned around you." He wasn't angry. I'd been scared of nothing. So, Irfan. Tell me honestly. How is that knee?

qa.q: How long did Joseph last in the final?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did young Joseph hide his ankle pain?
qa.a: He was eager and excited about the trophy, and scared the coach would think less of him or leave him out.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have changed Joseph's season?
qa.a: Telling the coach honestly about the sprain and resting, so the coach could plan around him instead of losing him for a season.

qa.q: How did Joseph's coach react when he finally heard the truth?
qa.a: The coach was not angry, more puzzled and disappointed, wishing Joseph had told him so he could plan around it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager hiding pain to play again and making the injury worse, and learning the coach would not have thought less of him for honesty.

passage: Six weeks after the cycling accident, Daniel still needed Zeynep to carry his coffee from the kitchen of their Hamburg flat. "I can do it," he snapped, and tried, and the mug slid off the crutch handle onto the floor. On Monday he had done double his physio exercises, sure it would speed things up, and spent Tuesday unable to bend his knee. On Wednesday he refused to do any at all and stayed in bed scrolling. "This is taking forever," he told Zeynep. She handed him the chart from the physio. "You said the same last week. Look, you're bending further than in March." Daniel looked at the numbers. Grudgingly, he set a timer for the ten-minute routine, just the amount the physio had set, and did it.

qa.q: What happened when Daniel tried to carry his own coffee?
qa.a: The mug slid off the crutch handle onto the floor.

qa.q: How was Daniel feeling about his recovery, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was impatient and annoyed, snapping at Zeynep and saying it was taking forever.

qa.q: What went wrong on Monday and Wednesday, and what works better?
qa.a: He overdid the exercises, then gave up entirely; doing the set routine steadily each day works better than either extreme.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeynep to help Daniel through this?
qa.a: It is probably tiring and a bit hurtful when he snaps, but she stays patient and points to his real progress.

grounding: Shows a young adult in recovery impatient and dependent, swinging between overdoing and giving up, and steady measured progress as the better path.

passage: For months after the auto overturned on the flyover, I couldn't sit in the back of one without my hands sweating. I'm Binita. The bruises healed in weeks, but the rest didn't. I took the long bus route to work, forty minutes extra, just to avoid that flyover. At night I'd hear the screech again and sit up. My cousin Dhruv noticed I'd stopped coming to Sunday lunch at his place across the river. "Is it the bridge?" he asked. I nodded, embarrassed. He didn't laugh. He rode with me once, holding my arm, and later helped me find a counsellor near my office. It took several sessions. Last month I crossed that flyover in an auto again. I held the rail the whole way, but I didn't get off.

qa.q: How much extra time did the long bus route take?
qa.a: Forty minutes extra.

qa.q: What does the long bus route tell you about how Binita felt?
qa.a: Binita still felt afraid and jumpy about the flyover, enough to avoid it every single day.

qa.q: What helped Binita's trust in the road return?
qa.a: Dhruv's patient company on a ride, time, and the counsellor Dhruv helped find when the fear lingered.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt when Binita stopped coming to Sunday lunch?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt worried and missed Binita, and cared enough to ask gently instead of teasing.

grounding: Shows a person after a road accident jumpy, avoiding the route and replaying the event, with time, support and a counsellor helping trust return.

passage: When Vidya broke her wrist falling on the metro steps last winter, my first instinct was to do everything for her. I'm Zeenat, we share a flat in Pune, and I'd already started cutting her rotis into squares before I caught myself. She was glaring. So I asked instead: "What do you want help with, and what do you want to do yourself?" She wanted help with her hair and the gas cylinder, nothing else. On bad days she cried with frustration over buttons, and I didn't say "at least it wasn't your head". I just sat on the floor and let her rant. When she managed her own ponytail in week five, I made a ridiculous fuss and she threw a sock at me. We still laugh about it.

qa.q: What did Vidya want help with?
qa.a: Her hair and the gas cylinder, nothing else.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when Vidya cried over buttons, and what did Zeenat do?
qa.a: Zeenat likely felt sad and helpless watching, but stayed calm and sat on the floor to listen instead of fixing or minimising it.

qa.q: Which of Zeenat's choices were supportive?
qa.a: Asking what help was wanted, listening to rants without saying it could have been worse, and celebrating the ponytail.

qa.q: How might Vidya have felt when her rotis were cut into squares?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and a bit humiliated at being treated as helpless when she wanted to do what she could.

grounding: Shows a helper offering practical support, listening to frustration without rushing it, celebrating small gains and letting the injured person do what she can.
